title: Leave room to respond

approved_context_blocks.**Approximate exercise model · Keep the: **Approximate exercise model · Keep the methods separate.** Define v as speed in km/h and t as the supplied reaction time in seconds. Exact constant-speed reaction distance is (v ÷ 3.6) × t metres; braking is not included. When an exercise specifies the rough method below, use both rough estimates together rather than substituting an exact reaction value.
approved_context_blocks.**Rough reaction estimate:**: **Rough reaction estimate:** R = (v ÷ 10) × t × 3 metres. Divide speed by ten, multiply by the supplied seconds, then by three. [Trafiko: approximate stopping method][stopping-shortcut] documents the one-second shortcut; multiplication by a supplied t is editorial proportional arithmetic. Half a second gives half the one-second estimate; two seconds gives twice it. These are supplied exercise inputs, not claims about every driver's reaction time.
approved_context_blocks.**Rough braking estimate:**: **Rough braking estimate:** B = (v ÷ 10)² × 0.4 metres. Divide speed by ten, square that result, then multiply by 0.4. [Trafiko: approximate stopping method][stopping-shortcut] describes this shortcut under good-brake, good-tyre and dry-asphalt assumptions. The coefficient is an exercise assumption, not a universal result for a real car or road. Supplied reaction time does not change the braking part in this model.
approved_context_blocks.**Rough total:**: **Rough total:** S = R + B. Calculate both parts separately with metres, then add. Keep decimal precision during the working; round only the final result if a precision is requested. These shortcuts teach arithmetic, not a safe-distance guarantee or a prediction for an actual hazard.
approved_context_blocks.**Source and assumption limits.**: **Source and assumption limits.** Trafiko is a commercial teaching source, cited only for these approximate shortcuts. [Trafikverket: stopping-distance principles][stopping-principles] supports reaction plus braking and dependence on speed and conditions, but does not supply these constants. Its illustrated distances have different assumptions and must not be mixed with this model. Real stopping depends on grip, gradient, tyres, brakes, response and other conditions. Retain the exact conversion and separate constant-deceleration comparison above under their own assumptions.
approved_context_blocks.**Worked approximate examples · Calculat: **Worked approximate examples · Calculate both parts.** Use the rough exercise equations consistently; each reaction time below is a supplied hypothetical input.
approved_context_blocks.**Example B · 70 km/h and one second.**: **Example B · 70 km/h and one second.** First v ÷ 10 = 7. Reaction R = 7 × 1 × 3 = 21 m. Braking B = 7² × 0.4 = 19.6 m. Total S = 21 + 19.6 = **40.6 m**. Squaring seven gives 49; do not multiply speed itself by 0.4.
